children.text: This lesson introduces no new mechanics. It consolidates every check this course has built, across explicit costs, slippage and impact, turnover and break-even, and methodology integrity, into one checklist to run before trusting any backtest enough to trade on it.

body.title: Explicit Cost Checks
steps: Brokerage modeled against your actual or intended broker's real fee schedule, including any flat-or-percentage, whichever-is-lower rule.
STT, exchange transaction charges, SEBI fees, and stamp duty modeled per segment, delivery, intraday, futures, and options each have different rates.
GST applied only to brokerage, exchange charges, and SEBI fees, never to STT or stamp duty.
All rates sourced from current broker or exchange circulars, not carried over from an old reference without checking for changes such as the October 2024 F&O STT increase.

body.title: Slippage and Impact Checks
steps: Spread cost calibrated to each stock's actual liquidity tier, not one flat number applied across large-cap and small-cap trades alike.
Market impact modeled from order size relative to average daily traded value, using the square-root law or an equivalent, not folded into brokerage or ignored.
Average daily traded value sourced per stock, per day, not a single static estimate for the entire backtest period.
Strategy-specific execution effects considered where relevant, such as momentum drift cost for signals that chase an already-moving price.

body.title: Turnover and Break-Even Checks
steps: Portfolio turnover ratio, or equivalently average holding period, computed for the strategy exactly as implemented, not assumed.
Break-even gross CAGR calculated as turnover ratio multiplied by round-trip cost.
A 2x to 3x safety margin required above break-even before treating the strategy as live-ready, not bare break-even.
Cost and impact assumptions re-checked at the actual capital size intended for live trading, not the backtest's default or convenient size.

body.title: Methodology Integrity Checks
steps: No fundamental or corporate action data used before its actual public availability date.
Fills assigned realistically, such as the next session's open after a close-based signal, never the same bar as the signal itself.
Backtest universe reflects historical index membership at each point in time, not today's membership applied retroactively.
The cost model is applied inside every backtest run used for strategy selection, never bolted on only to the already-chosen final candidate.

body.caption: What each category costs you if skipped

cells: In the Bank Nifty scalping case study, transaction costs alone consumed 91.3% of gross profit

children.text: Run all four categories before every go or no-go decision, not as a box-ticking formality but as an actual gate a strategy has to clear. Re-run the relevant sections whenever anything material changes, a new universe, a change in intended capital, a different rebalance frequency, since each of those changes what the checklist's own numbers would say.

body.text: Notice that none of these four categories are optional add-ons to a working backtest, each one is the subject of an entire chapter in this course because each one has, on its own, been shown to turn a profitable-looking strategy into an unprofitable one.

body.title: Quick Check
body.question: A colleague says their backtest is trustworthy because they carefully modeled brokerage, STT, and GST using current rates. Based on this course, is that sufficient?
options: Yes, explicit costs are the only thing that matters for backtest realism
No, explicit costs are only Category 1 of four; slippage and market impact, turnover and break-even discipline, and methodology integrity each independently have the power to invalidate a backtest
No, but only because GST rates change too often to model reliably
Yes, as long as the strategy trades cash equity and not F&O
body.explanation: Explicit costs are necessary but not sufficient. This course showed slippage and market impact, turnover-driven cost drag, and methodology bugs like look-ahead bias and unrealistic fills each independently capable of turning a profitable-looking backtest into a losing live strategy, entirely separate from whether brokerage and STT were modeled correctly.

body.text: A trustworthy backtest is not one clever fix, it is four independent disciplines holding at once: explicit costs priced correctly, slippage and impact modeled by liquidity, turnover kept under break-even with a real safety margin, and the underlying methodology free of look-ahead bias and unrealistic fills. Skip any one category and the other three cannot save you.

points: A cost-aware backtest checklist has four independent categories: explicit costs, slippage and market impact, turnover and break-even discipline, and methodology integrity, each covered by its own chapter in this course.
Every category in this checklist was shown, in a dedicated case study, to be capable of turning a profitable-looking backtest into an unprofitable live strategy on its own.
The checklist should be run as an actual go/no-go gate before live capital is committed, and re-run whenever the strategy's universe, capital size, or rebalance frequency changes materially.

Modeling explicit costs correctly, while necessary, is not sufficient on its own, a backtest can still fail from unmodeled slippage, excessive turnover, or methodology bugs even with a perfect cost stack.
